chapters.t: The reader, his two transmitters and the way of the Durrah
p: The reader: Abū Jaʿfar Yazīd ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ al-Makhzūmī al-Madanī (d. 130 AH) was one of the Successors and one of the teachers of Imām Nāfiʿ. He learned the Qurʾān from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAyyāsh, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Hurayrah.
The transmitters: His reading was preserved by two students, ʿĪsā ibn Wardān (d. 160 AH) and Sulaymān ibn Muslim ibn Jammāz (d. 170 AH).

The way: These principles follow al-Durrah al-Muḍiyyah, the poem in which Ibn al-Jazarī added three readers to the seven of the Shāṭibiyyah. The Durrah treats Nāfiʿ as the base (aṣl) of Abū Jaʿfar and mentions only the places where Abū Jaʿfar departs from that base.
Istiʿādhah: No rule special to Abū Jaʿfar is recorded. The Durrah does not discuss the istiʿādhah, because the three readers agree with their base readers on it.

Basmalah between two surahs: When he joins the end of one surah to the beginning of the next he always recites the basmalah between them. The only exception is the start of Sūrat al-Tawbah, which has no basmalah.

Verse count of al-Fātiḥah: Unlike Ḥafṣ, he does not count the basmalah as an ayah. The first ayah is ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ, and the last ayah of Ḥafṣ is divided in two: صِرَٰطَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمُۥ is ayah 6 and غَيْرِ ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمُۥ وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ is ayah 7.
The word مَلِكِ: He reads مَلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ without an alif after the mīm, where Ḥafṣ reads مَٰلِكِ.

Before a vowelled letter: In connected recitation he gives every mīm al-jamʿ a ḍammah followed by a wāw of two ḥarakāt (ṣilah). This is his only way, for both transmitters. Examples: رَبُّهُمُۥ, إِنَّهُمُۥ كَانُوا, وَجِلَتْ قُلُوبُهُمُۥ. Ḥafṣ reads the mīm with sukūn.
Before hamzat al-qaṭʿ: The wāw of the ṣilah then counts as a madd munfaṣil, so it stays at two ḥarakāt, as in وَٱجْتَبَيْنَٰهُمُۥ وَهَدَيْنَٰهُمُۥ إِلَىٰ صِرَٰطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.
Before a sākin letter: The mīm takes a short ḍammah without ṣilah, as with the other readers: مِنْهُمُ ٱلْمُومِنُونَ وَأَكْثَرُهُمُ ٱلْفَٰسِقُونَ.
In waqf: When he stops on mīm al-jamʿ it is sākinah.

Hāʾ read with sukūn: Both transmitters read the hāʾ sākinah in يُوَدِّهْ إِلَيْكَ (both occurrences in 3:75), نُوتِهْ مِنْهَا (3:145 and 42:20), نُوَلِّهْ مَا تَوَلَّىٰ وَنُصْلِهْ جَهَنَّمَ (4:115) and فَأَلْقِهْ إِلَيْهِمْ (27:28). Ḥafṣ reads all of these with kasrah and ṣilah except the last, where he also has sukūn.
The word يَاتِهِۦ: In وَمَن يَاتِهِۦ مُومِنًا (20:75) he reads the hāʾ with kasrah and ṣilah.

The word وَيَتَّقِهِ (24:52): Abū Jaʿfar reads the qāf with kasrah. Ibn Wardān reads the hāʾ sākinah, وَيَتَّقِهْ, and Ibn Jammāz reads it with kasrah and ṣilah, وَيَتَّقِهِۦ. Ḥafṣ alone reads the qāf sākinah and the hāʾ with a short kasrah, وَيَتَّقْهِ.
The word يَرْضَهُ (39:7): The reverse holds here. Ibn Wardān reads ḍammah with ṣilah, يَرْضَهُۥ لَكُمْ, and Ibn Jammāz reads the hāʾ sākinah, يَرْضَهْ لَكُمْ.

The word أَرْجِهِ (7:111 and 26:36): Ibn Wardān reads the hāʾ with a short kasrah without ṣilah, أَرْجِهِ وَأَخَاهُ, and Ibn Jammāz reads it with ṣilah, أَرْجِهِۦ وَأَخَاهُ. Ḥafṣ reads أَرْجِهْ with sukūn.
The word تُرْزَقَانِهِ (12:37): Ibn Wardān reads the hāʾ with a short kasrah without ṣilah; Ibn Jammāz reads it with ṣilah, تُرْزَقَانِهِۦ.

Kasrah where Ḥafṣ has ḍammah: He reads وَمَا أَنسَىٰنِيهِ إِلَّا ٱلشَّيْطَٰنُ (18:63) and بِمَا عَٰهَدَ عَلَيْهِ ٱللَّهَ (48:10) with kasrah on the hāʾ, and in the second the lām of the Name of Allah is therefore light (tarqīq). Ḥafṣ reads ḍammah in both.
The phrase فِيهِ مُهَانًا (25:69): He reads the hāʾ with a short kasrah, without the ṣilah that Ḥafṣ has here.
Madd muttaṣil: He lengthens it to a medium length (tawassuṭ) of four ḥarakāt, as in شَآءَ, سُوٓءَ and جَزَآؤُهُمْ.
Madd munfaṣil: He reads it with qaṣr, two ḥarakāt, as in يَا أَيُّهَا, قَالُوا إِنَّا and فِي أُمِّهَا. Ḥafṣ lengthens it.

The pronoun أَنَا: When it is followed by a hamzat al-qaṭʿ carrying fatḥah or ḍammah, he pronounces its alif in connected recitation and gives it two ḥarakāt as a madd munfaṣil, as in أَنَا أُحْيِي وَأُمِيتُ and وَأَنَا أَوَّلُ ٱلْمُسْلِمِينَ. Ḥafṣ drops this alif when connecting.

أَنَا before kasrah or another letter: When the following hamzah carries kasrah, or any letter other than hamzah follows, he drops the alif in connected recitation exactly as Ḥafṣ does, as in إِنْ أَنَا إِلَّا نَذِيرٌ.

General rule: When the interrogative hamzah is followed by a second hamzat al-qaṭʿ in the same word, he pronounces the first fully, softens the second (tashīl, a sound between hamzah and the madd letter that matches its vowel) and inserts an alif between the two (idkhāl), as Qālūn does. This applies whether the second hamzah has fatḥah, kasrah or ḍammah: ءَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ, أَءِذَا, أَءُنزِلَ. The source also lists أَئِمَّةً among these words. Ḥafṣ pronounces both hamzahs fully with no alif.
The word أَءُشْهِدُوا (43:19): He reads it with two hamzahs, the second with ḍammah and the shīn sākinah, applying tashīl of the second hamzah with idkhāl. Ḥafṣ reads أَشَهِدُوا.
Tashīl without idkhāl: In ءَامَنتُمْ (7:123, 20:71 and 26:49) and ءَأَٰلِهَتُنَا (43:58) he softens the second hamzah but does not insert an alif.

Added interrogative hamzah: He reads ءَأَذْهَبْتُمْ (46:20) and ءَأَن كَانَ (68:14) as questions with two hamzahs, following the general rule; Ḥafṣ has one hamzah in each. He also reads ءَآلسِّحْرُ (10:81) as a question; the hamzat al-waṣl after the interrogative hamzah is either turned into an alif with madd lāzim or softened.
Dropped interrogative hamzah: He reads إِنَّكَ لَأَنتَ يُوسُفُ (12:90) as a statement with one hamzah.

Repeated question (istifhām mukarrar): In the eleven passages where two questions of the type أَءِذَا ... أَءِنَّا come together, he reads the first as a statement with one hamzah and the second as a question, for example إِذَا كُنَّا تُرَٰبًا أَءِنَّا لَفِي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ (13:5). The passages are 13:5, 17:49, 17:98, 23:82, 27:67, 29:28-29, 32:10, 37:16, 37:53, 56:47 and 79:10-11.
Exceptions to the repeated question: In 37:16 and 56:47 he does the opposite, a question first and a statement second: أَءِذَا مِتْنَا وَكُنَّا تُرَابًا وَعِظَٰمًا إِنَّا لَمَبْعُوثُونَ.

Same vowel: When the hamzah ending one word and the hamzah beginning the next carry the same vowel, he softens the second (tashīl). Examples: جَآءَ أَمْرُنَا, هَٰؤُلَآءِ إِن, أَوْلِيَآءُ أُولَٰئِكَ (the only case with two ḍammahs). Ḥafṣ pronounces both fully, here and in all the cases below.
First hamzah with fatḥah: If the first has fatḥah and the second has kasrah or ḍammah, he softens the second, as in تَفِيٓءَ إِلَىٰ and جَآءَ أُمَّةً.

Second hamzah with fatḥah: He changes the second (ibdāl) into a wāw with fatḥah after ḍammah, as in ٱلسُّفَهَآءُ أَلَا read ٱلسُّفَهَآءُ وَلَا, and into a yāʾ with fatḥah after kasrah, as in مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ ءَايَةً read ٱلسَّمَآءِ يَايَةً.

Ḍammah followed by kasrah: As in يَشَآءُ إِلَىٰ, he has two ways for the second hamzah: ibdāl into a wāw with kasrah (يَشَآءُ وِلَىٰ), which is given precedence, or tashīl. The reverse order does not occur in the Qurʾān.
Stopping on the first word: If he stops on the first word, he begins the second with a full hamzah.

Sākin hamzah: He turns every sākin hamzah into the madd letter that matches the vowel before it (ibdāl), as in مُومِنٌ, يَاكُلُ, ٱقْرَا and مُوصَدَةٌ, and also across two words, as in لِقَآءَنَا ٱيتِ. Ḥafṣ keeps the hamzah.
Exceptions: He keeps the sākin hamzah in أَنۢبِئْهُم (2:33) and وَنَبِّئْهُمْ (15:51 and 54:28).
Ibdāl with idghām: In ٱلرُّءْيَا and all its forms, and in وَرِءْيًا, the hamzah becomes a yāʾ that is merged into the next yāʾ: ٱلرُّيَّا, لِلرُّيَّا, وَرِيًّا.

Hamzah with fatḥah after ḍammah: When it is the first root letter he changes it into a wāw, as in مُوَجَّلًا, وَٱلْمُوَلَّفَةِ and مُوَذِّنٌ. In يُؤَيِّدُ (3:13) Ibn Jammāz makes this ibdāl, يُوَيِّدُ, while Ibn Wardān keeps the hamzah.

Hamzah with fatḥah after kasrah: In a set list of words he changes it into a yāʾ: مِايَةٌ, فِيَةٌ, مِايَتَيْنِ, فِيَتَيْنِ, قُرِيَ, رِيَآءَ, شَانِيَكَ, خَاطِيَةٍ, ٱسْتُهْزِيَ, نَاشِيَةَ, لَيُبَطِّيَنَّ, مُلِيَتْ, خَاسِيًا and لَنُبَوِّيَنَّهُمْ. In مَوْطِئًا (9:120) both ibdāl and the hamzah are transmitted from him.
Hamzah changed to alif: He reads سَالَ (70:1) and مِنسَاتَهُ with an alif in place of the hamzah.
The words of prophethood and ٱلذِّيبُ: He reads ٱلنَّبِيُّ, ٱلنَّبِيِّينَ, ٱلْأَنۢبِيَآءَ and ٱلنُّبُوَّةَ without hamzah, and reads ٱلذِّيبُ with ibdāl, but keeps the hamzah of لِئَلَّا.
Dropped hamzah after fatḥah: A hamzah with ḍammah followed by wāw is dropped and the fatḥah before it stays: يَطَوْنَ, لَمْ تَطَوْهَا, أَن تَطَوْهُمْ.

Dropped hamzah after kasrah: A hamzah with ḍammah followed by wāw is dropped and its ḍammah moves to the letter before it: مُسْتَهْزُونَ, وَٱلصَّٰبُونَ, مُتَّكُونَ, فَمَالُونَ, أَنۢبُونِي, لِيُطْفُوا, لِيُوَاطُوا. Ḥafṣ reads مُسْتَهْزِءُونَ and وَٱلصَّٰبِـُٔونَ.
The word ٱلْمُنشِـُٔونَ (56:72): Ibn Jammāz drops the hamzah, ٱلْمُنشُونَ; Ibn Wardān has both ways.
Dropped hamzah before yāʾ: A hamzah with kasrah after kasrah and before yāʾ is dropped in وَٱلصَّٰبِينَ, ٱلْخَٰطِينَ, ٱلْمُسْتَهْزِينَ and مُتَّكِينَ. He also drops the hamzah of مُتَّكًا (12:31).

Hamzah merged into the letter before it: He reads جُزًّا and جُزٌّ with a doubled zāy and no hamzah, كَهَيَّةِ with a doubled yāʾ, and ٱلنَّسِيُّ with a doubled yāʾ. Ḥafṣ reads جُزْءًا, كَهَيْـَٔةِ and ٱلنَّسِيٓءُ.

Tashīl in particular words: He softens the second hamzah of أَرَأَيْتَ and its forms; he reads هَٰأَنتُمْ with an alif and a softened hamzah; he softens the hamzah of إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ; and he reads كَأَيِّن as كَآئِن, with an alif after the kāf and a softened hamzah. Before the softened hamzah of the last two words the alif may be given four or two ḥarakāt.

The word ٱلَّٰٓـِٔي (in surahs 33, 58 and 65): He reads it without the final yāʾ. When connecting, the hamzah is softened and the alif before it has four or two ḥarakāt. When stopping, he either changes the hamzah into a sākin yāʾ with a madd of six ḥarakāt, or softens it with rawm, the alif again having four or two ḥarakāt.

Hamzah where Ḥafṣ has none: He reads هُزُؤًا and كُفُؤًا with hamzah where Ḥafṣ has a wāw, and reads وَرَبَأَتْ with a hamzah after the bāʾ. He reads زَكَرِيَّآءَ with a hamzah and madd muttaṣil, and مِيكَآئِلَ with a hamzah after the alif.
Naql in general: Abū Jaʿfar does not move the vowel of a hamzah to a preceding sākin letter (naql) except in the few words below.
The word رِدًا (28:34): Where Ḥafṣ reads رِدْءًا, he reads رِدَا, with fatḥah on the dāl followed by an alif and no hamzah, without tanwīn, both when connecting and when stopping.
The phrase مِنِ ٱجْلِ ذَٰلِكَ (5:32): He alone reads the hamzah with kasrah and moves that kasrah to the nūn, dropping the hamzah.

The phrase عَادًا ٱلْأُولَىٰ (53:50): He moves the ḍammah of the hamzah to the lām and merges the tanwīn into that lām: عَادًا لُّولَىٰ. If he stops on عَادًا, he may begin the next word in three ways: ٱلْأُولَىٰ as Ḥafṣ, ٱلُولَىٰ with hamzat al-waṣl and a lām with ḍammah, or لُولَىٰ without hamzat al-waṣl.
The word ٱلْـَٰٔنَ: Ibn Wardān reads it with naql wherever it occurs, ٱلَٰنَ (for example 2:71, 2:187, 4:18, 72:9); Ibn Jammāz reads it without naql, like Ḥafṣ.

The word ءَآلْـَٰٔنَ (10:51 and 10:91): The hamzat al-waṣl after the interrogative hamzah is read in two ways, as an alif with a madd of six ḥarakāt, or softened. Ibn Jammāz reads these without naql. Ibn Wardān adds naql and so has three ways: ibdāl with six ḥarakāt, ibdāl with two ḥarakāt, or tashīl.
The phrase مِلْءُ ٱلْأَرْضِ (3:91): Ibn Wardān reads it with naql, مِلُ ٱلْأَرْضِ; Ibn Jammāz reads it like Ḥafṣ.
The sakt of Ḥafṣ: He does not make the four pauses of Ḥafṣ at عِوَجًا قَيِّمًا (18:1-2), مَرْقَدِنَا هَٰذَا (36:52), مَنْ رَاقٍ (75:27) and بَلْ رَانَ (83:14); he connects them.

Sakt on the opening letters: He makes a short pause without breath (sakt) on each of the separate letters at the openings of surahs, as in الٓمٓ, الٓمٓصٓ, الٓر, طسٓمٓ and كٓهيعٓصٓ. Each letter keeps its own length: the alif has no madd, letters with the madd sign have six ḥarakāt, and the letters ḥāʾ, yāʾ, ṭāʾ, hāʾ and rāʾ have two. Because of this sakt the nūn is read clearly in يسٓ وَٱلْقُرْءَانِ and نٓ وَٱلْقَلَمِ.
The word تَأْمَنَّا (12:11): He alone reads it with a complete idghām of the two nūns, without rawm or ishmām, and with ibdāl of the hamzah: تَامَنَّا.
Dhāl into tāʾ: He merges the dhāl into the tāʾ in عُذْتُ (40:27 and 44:20) and in ٱتَّخَذْتُمْ, أَخَذْتُمْ and their forms wherever they occur. Ḥafṣ reads them with iẓhār.
Thāʾ into tāʾ: He merges the thāʾ into the tāʾ in لَبِثْتَ, لَبِثْتُ and لَبِثْتُمْ.
The words فَنَبَذْتُهَا (20:96) and أُورِثْتُمُوهَا: The secondary source states that he reads these two with iẓhār.
Iẓhār in two places: He reads يَلْهَثْ ذَٰلِكَ (7:176) and ٱرْكَبْ مَعَنَا (11:42) with iẓhār, where Ḥafṣ has idghām.
The standard small idghām letters: He reads with iẓhār the dhāl of إِذْ, the dāl of قَدْ, the feminine tāʾ and the lām of هَلْ and بَلْ before their letters.

Ikhfāʾ before ghayn and khāʾ: Abū Jaʿfar alone hides the nūn sākinah and the tanwīn (ikhfāʾ) before ghayn and khāʾ, as in مِنْ غَيْرِكُمْ, مِنْ خَلْفِهِمْ and حَلِيمًا غَفُورًا. Ḥafṣ reads them with iẓhār.
Exceptions: He reads with iẓhār in three places: فَسَيُنْغِضُونَ (17:51), وَٱلْمُنْخَنِقَةُ (5:3) and إِن يَكُنْ غَنِيًّا (4:135).
The word يَٰأَبَتَ: When he stops on this word, which is written with an open tāʾ, he stops with a hāʾ: يَٰأَبَهْ. Ḥafṣ stops with a tāʾ.
General rule: He reads the yāʾāt al-iḍāfah as Qālūn does, except in three places.
وَلِي دِينِ (109:6): He reads the yāʾ sākinah, where Ḥafṣ reads وَلِيَ دِينِ with fatḥah.
إِخْوَتِيَ إِنَّ (12:100): He reads the yāʾ with fatḥah in connected recitation; Ḥafṣ reads it sākinah.
رَبِّيَ إِنَّ لِي (41:50): He reads the yāʾ with fatḥah; Ḥafṣ reads it sākinah.
General rule: In the places below he pronounces an unwritten yāʾ when connecting and drops it when stopping. Ḥafṣ drops it in both cases.
ٱلتَّلَاقِ (40:15) and ٱلتَّنَادِ (40:32): Ibn Wardān pronounces the yāʾ when connecting; Ibn Jammāz drops it, like Ḥafṣ.
يَٰعِبَادِي لَا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْكُمُ (43:68): He pronounces the yāʾ both when connecting and when stopping. Ḥafṣ reads يَٰعِبَادِ without it.

Yāʾ with fatḥah: The source lists three further words apart from the rest: أَلَّا تَتَّبِعَنِ (20:93), فَمَا ءَاتَىٰنِ (27:36) and إِن يُرِدْنِ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنُ (36:23). He pronounces the yāʾ in them when connecting. The Durrah line quoted by the source says that in يُرِدْنِ, and likewise تَتَّبِعَنِ, he adds the yāʾ with fatḥah and keeps a yāʾ in both states, that is, when stopping too.

Meeting of two sākin letters: When the first sākin is followed by a verb that begins with hamzat al-waṣl and whose third letter has a permanent ḍammah, he gives the first sākin a ḍammah: قُلُ ٱدْعُوا, وَقَالَتُ ٱخْرُجْ, أَنُ ٱعْبُدُوا. Ḥafṣ gives it a kasrah.
The word ٱضْطِرَّ: In فَمَنُ ٱضْطِرَّ he reads the ṭāʾ with kasrah instead of ḍammah.
لِلْمَلَٰئِكَةُ ٱسْجُدُوا: He reads the tāʾ with ḍammah instead of kasrah when connecting.
Ishmām: He reads سِيٓءَ (11:77) and سِيٓـَٔتْ (67:27) with ishmām, mixing the kasrah of the sīn with a rounding of the lips toward ḍammah.
The word خُطْوَٰتِ: He reads the ṭāʾ sākinah wherever it occurs; Ḥafṣ reads خُطُوَٰتِ.
Ḍammah on the middle letter: He reads نُكُرًا, فَسُحُقًا, ٱلْعُسُرَ, يُسُرًا, لِلْعُسُرَىٰ, لِلْيُسُرَىٰ and ٱلرُّعُبَ with ḍammah where Ḥafṣ has sukūn.
The pronoun هُوَ: He reads its hāʾ sākinah after wāw, fāʾ, lām and ثُمَّ: وَهْوَ, فَهْوَ, لَهْوَ, ثُمَّ هْوَ.
The word عَشَرَ: He reads its ʿayn sākinah, as in تِسْعَةَ عْشَرَ (74:30) and ٱثْنَآ عْشَرَ (9:36); in the second the alif takes a madd lāzim of six ḥarakāt.
لَا يَخْرُجُ (7:58): Ibn Wardān has two ways, لَا يُخْرِجُ with ḍammah on the yāʾ and kasrah on the rāʾ, or like Ḥafṣ. Ibn Jammāz reads like Ḥafṣ.
لَسْتَ مُومِنًا (4:94): Ibn Wardān reads the second mīm with fatḥah, مُومَنًا; Ibn Jammāz reads it with kasrah.
سِقَايَةَ ٱلْحَآجِّ (9:19): Ibn Jammāz reads سِقَايَةَ ٱلْحَآجِّ وَعِمَارَةَ ٱلْمَسْجِدِ like Ḥafṣ. Ibn Wardān has this and a second way, سُقَاةَ ٱلْحَآجِّ وَعَمَرَةَ ٱلْمَسْجِدِ.
فَيُغْرِقَكُمْ (17:69): Abū Jaʿfar reads ٱلرِّيَٰحِ in the plural and فَتُغْرِقَكُمْ with tāʾ. Ibn Wardān has a second way with a doubled rāʾ, فَتُغَرِّقَكُمْ.
يَٰحَسْرَتَىٰ (39:56): He adds a yāʾ after the alif. Ibn Jammāz reads it with fatḥah, يَٰحَسْرَتَايَ; Ibn Wardān has this and a second way with a sākin yāʾ and a long madd, يَٰحَسْرَتَآيْ.
